title: Preparation of Flexible Material from Mycelium of Wood-Decaying Fungi
author: Vadivel, Dondi
materials: MTS Insight Electromechanical Testing Systems 10 kN

3.Extraction of alkali-insolubles.a.Wash the biomass obtained after cultivation with water; this removes the residues of the medium and extracellular compounds produced by the fungus.b.Filter the contents through a nylon filtration bag.c.Blend the biomass using a sterile metal blender.d.Keep the blended biomass in hot water at 90 °C for 1 hour, which removes water-soluble compounds.e.After partially cooling down, filter the biomass using nylon filtration bags.f.Wash and filter the biomass several times.g.Resuspend the recovered biomass in 1.5 L of water.h.Blend the mixture until it is homogeneous.i.Add 3.5% w/w of Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to the solution.j.Incubate the mixture for 2 hours at 65 °C. This procedure is followed to eliminate proteins and alkali-soluble carbohydrates.k.Allow the mixture to cool to ambient temperature.l.Filter the mixture with a nylon filtration bag.m.Wash the biomass multiple times to reduce the pH to neutral.n.Drain the biomass completely and recover.o.Resuspend the biomass in water to form an alkali-insoluble slurry.
CRITICAL: Drain the contents completely during the last cycle of washing, it is necessary for maximising the recovery of biomass from the filtration bag.
4.Crosslinking and Plasticization of biomass.a.Add 1% acetic acid and 10% glycerol to a 3L final volume to the alkali-insoluble slurry.b.Blend the mixture to avoid coagulation and promote homogeneity.c.Incubate the obtained creamy mixture in a water bath at 60 °C for 4 hours.d.Pour the slurry on a filter paper sheet kept on the vacuum table of size (21 cm x 29.7 cm).e.Transfer the solid part to plastic foil (34.5 cm x 34.5 cm) and dry for 48 hours.
CRITICAL: It is important to wait till complete drying of the slurry using vacuum, as the slurry is thick and might not lose water.
Note: During the sodium hydroxide treatment step, a partial deacetylation of chitin can occur, leading to free amine groups. The addition of acetic acid protonates amine groups, creating positively charged groups that increase the chain interaction through dipole-induced dipole forces, which enhances the stability of the mycelium mats, rather than being brittle in the presence of chitin. In this case, we can not expect the acetic acid to readily dissolve the material6,7 because the naturally packed structure of the polymers does not allow it. The introduction of glycerol improves the flexibility of the mycelium mats through the formation of hydrogen bonds with chitin and beta-glucan backbones, which significantly affects the mechanical properties.8 The right tuning with the acetic acid that brings stability and glycerol that brings flexibility is the key.

Figure 1A shows the mycelium mat containing only glycerol plasticizer, the sharp peak around 1028 cm-1 corresponds to C-O bond stretching of secondary alcohol in glycerol which is also a characteristic peak.9
Figure 1B shows the mycelium mat containing only acetic acid as crosslinking agent, the sharp peak around 1748 cm-1 represents the C=O stretching frequency which is a characteristic peak in acetic acid.10
Figure 1C shows the mycelium mats containing both characteristic peaks of acetic acid and glycerol shows preliminary crosslinking and plasticization effect which could be confirmed further by mechanical properties experiments.5.Thermogravimetric Analysis.a.Set the conditions in TGA as 25 °C to 800 °C by the heating rate of 20 °C/min under Nitrogen atmospheric conditions with a mass flow rate of 100 mL/min.b.Perform a Blank with an empty crucible.c.Add 8-10 mg of sample and run the experiment.d.Analyse the data as follows,i.Complete the experiment and analyse the data using the StarE software.ii.Take the first derivative of the analysed sample.iii.Plot the data as a function of % of weight loss vs temperature.6.Mechanical testing system.a.Cut rectangular specimens (110 mm × 10 mm) specimen of the formed sheets.b.Set pneumatic grips 50 mm apart from each other.c.Use 250 N load cells.d.Set the separation of jaws at a uniform speed of 2 mm/min, this was to ensure quasi-static conditions.e.Measure each sample with a digital calliper and take the weight of the sample before mechanical testing to estimate its density.f.Test the samples and analyse the data as follows,i.Calculate the tensile strength Tn (in MPa) Tn=Fwt where F is the highest force recorded during the test (in N), w is the specimen width (in mm), and t is the specimen thickness (in mm).ii.Calculate the percentage elongation εp to a specified load value, with εp = L−L0L0 100 where L is the separation of the jaws and L0 is the initial separation of the jaws.7.Dynamic mechanical analysis.a.Produce the specimen with 0.8 mm thickness.b.Set the frequency as 1 Hz.c.Measure Storage (E′, G′) and loss (E″, G″) moduli as a function of temperature in the 20°C/200°C range.Figure 1FTIR of mycelium mat with glycerol, acetic acid, and bothFTIR of mycelium mat with glycerol alone (A), FTIR of mycelium mat with acetic acid alone (B), FTIR of mycelium mat with both glycerol and acetic acid (C).

steps.title: Select fungal strain with high chitin
steps.instruction: Determine chitin, α‑glucan and β‑glucan content of candidate wood‑decay fungal strains using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM); choose a strain that shows high levels of these polymers.

steps.title: Cultivate fungal biomass
steps.instruction: Scale up the fungus through three stages – plate culture, flask culture, and bioreactor culture – using identical liquid medium composition (malt extract 2 %, dextrose 0.5 %, yeast extract 0.2 %). Maintain sterility throughout.

substeps.instruction: a) Plate culture: Grow the strain on 2 % malt extract agar in 9 cm Petri plates for 10 days; cut 0.5 cm² mycelium plugs from active colonies; transfer plugs into 0.1 L sterilised liquid broth (2 % malt, 0.5 % dextrose, 0.2 % yeast extract); incubate in a shaker at 181 rpm, 25 °C, dark for 7 days; blend the culture with a sterile metal blender.

b) Flask scale‑up: Transfer the blended culture to a larger flask containing 0.5 L sterilised broth (same composition); store 3 days; blend again after 3 days; withdraw 33 mL of the creamy mixture and add to a second flask containing 1.2 L sterilised broth (same composition); incubate in a shaker at 181 rpm, 25 °C for 7 days.

c) Bioreactor scale‑up: Transfer the blended culture to a flask with 1 L sterilised broth (same composition); store 3 days; blend after 3 days; move the blend into a 10 L bioreactor containing 10 L sterilised broth (same composition); add 2 mL sunflower oil (to limit foam); run the bioreactor at 25 °C, 50 % oxygen saturation, aeration 5–20 L min⁻¹, agitation 80–150 rpm for 7 days.

steps.title: Extract alkali‑insoluble material
steps.instruction: Wash, filter, blend, and chemically treat the harvested mycelial biomass to obtain an alkali‑insoluble slurry.

substeps.instruction: Wash the harvested biomass with water to remove medium residues and extracellular compounds.
Filter the washed biomass through a nylon filtration bag.
Blend the filtered biomass with a sterile metal blender.
Place the blended biomass in hot water at 90 °C for 1 hour to remove water‑soluble compounds.
After partial cooling, filter the hot mixture again through a nylon bag.
Wash and filter the biomass repeatedly.
Resuspend the recovered biomass in 1.5 L of water.
Blend the suspension until homogeneous.
Add sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to a final concentration of 3.5 % w/w.
Incubate the alkaline mixture for 2 hours at 65 °C to remove proteins and alkali‑soluble carbohydrates.
Allow the mixture to cool to ambient temperature.
Filter the cooled mixture with a nylon bag.
Wash the filtered biomass several times until the pH is neutral.
Drain the biomass completely (critical for maximal recovery).
Resuspend the drained biomass in water to form an alkali‑insoluble slurry.

steps.title: Crosslink and plasticize biomass
steps.instruction: Add crosslinker and plasticizer to the alkali‑insoluble slurry, incubate, and dry to obtain a flexible sheet.

substeps.instruction: Add acetic acid to a final concentration of 1 % and glycerol to 10 % (by weight) to the slurry, adjusting the total volume to 3 L.
Blend the mixture to prevent coagulation and ensure homogeneity.
Incubate the creamy mixture in a water bath at 60 °C for 4 hours.
Pour the slurry onto a filter‑paper sheet placed on a vacuum table (size 21 cm × 29.7 cm).
Transfer the resulting solid layer onto a plastic foil (34.5 cm × 34.5 cm) and dry under vacuum for 48 hours until completely dry.

steps.title: Perform thermogravimetric analysis
steps.instruction: Run TGA on the dried material and process the data.

substeps.instruction: Set TGA parameters: temperature range 25 °C to 800 °C, heating rate 20 °C min⁻¹, nitrogen atmosphere, gas flow 100 mL min⁻¹.
Run a blank measurement using an empty crucible.
Place 8–10 mg of the sample in a crucible and start the run.
Analyse the data: use StarE software, compute the first derivative of the weight‑loss curve, and plot % weight loss versus temperature.

steps.title: Mechanical tensile testing
steps.instruction: Cut specimens from the dried sheet and test their tensile properties.

substeps.instruction: Cut rectangular specimens 110 mm × 10 mm from the formed sheets.
Set pneumatic grips 50 mm apart on the testing machine.
Install a 250 N load cell.
Program the jaws to separate at a uniform speed of 2 mm min⁻¹ (quasi‑static conditions).
Measure each specimen’s width, thickness with a digital caliper and record its weight to estimate density.
Run the tensile test; then calculate:
i) Tensile strength Tₙ (MPa) using Tₙ = F w t, where F is the maximum force (N), w is specimen width (mm), and t is thickness (mm).
ii) Percentage elongation εₚ = (L − L₀) / L₀ × 100, where L is the final jaw separation and L₀ the initial separation.

steps.title: Dynamic mechanical analysis
steps.instruction: Measure visco‑elastic properties of the material over a temperature sweep.

substeps.instruction: Prepare a specimen with a thickness of 0.8 mm.
Set the oscillation frequency to 1 Hz.
Record storage (E′, G′) and loss (E″, G″) moduli while heating from 20 °C to 200 °C.
